claims.text: The initial material is nanocrystalline W38Ta36Cr15V11.
Nanocrystalline W38Ta36Cr15V11 forms Cr-V-rich precipitates under energetic-particle exposure near 8 dpa.
The intervention is a trace Zr addition during synthesis of nanocrystalline W38Ta36Cr15V11.
Zr will segregate to grain boundaries in the alloy.
Segregated Zr will stabilize the grain boundaries.
Grain-boundary Zr will alter diffusion kinetics and prevent nucleation of Cr-V-rich precipitates.
Zr will act as a solute trap that reduces the mobility of Cr and V atoms during irradiation.
The Zr addition will maintain the nanocrystalline structure.
The nanocrystalline structure underlies the alloy's low irradiation hardening.
The nanocrystalline structure underlies the alloy's high radiation resistance.
Trace Zr addition will not complicate bulk fabrication and will preserve practical bulk manufacturability.
At 8 dpa, the Zr-doped alloy will contain significantly fewer or no Cr-V-rich precipitates relative to the unmodified alloy.
At 8 dpa, the Zr-doped alloy will retain radiation resistance similar to that of the unmodified alloy.
At 8 dpa, the Zr-doped alloy will retain similarly low hardening relative to the unmodified alloy.
The unmodified nanocrystalline W38Ta36Cr15V11 baseline exhibits a hardening increase associated with Cr-V-rich precipitate formation at about 8 dpa.
The proposed suppression effect will remain effective up to approximately 8 dpa over 300–600°C.
Above approximately 8 dpa or outside 300–600°C, precipitate suppression may diminish or other damage modes may dominate.
A specimen-temperature range of 300–600°C is representative of fusion first-wall and divertor operating conditions.
The optimal Zr concentration for grain-boundary segregation without adverse effects is unknown.

contradictions.description: The baseline states that precipitate formation at about 8 dpa is associated with increased hardening, whereas the task premise describes W38Ta36Cr15V11 as showing negligible hardening despite precipitates appearing at 8 dpa.
